result.markdown: --- course-unit: ch11-interventions-and-optimization status: complete --- # Interventions and optimization ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 3, Session 2. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd). ::: An intervention model has two layers. First, a **scenario** specifies a policy and simulates its consequences. Second, an **optimization** compares many admissible policies using an explicit objective and constraints. Keeping those layers separate makes it possible to audit a proposed policy before asking an optimizer to choose one. ## Learning goals By the end of this chapter you should be able to: - represent a temporary reduction in transmission with an ODE callback; - distinguish a callback-driven scenario from an optimization problem; - formulate a small bounded intervention-timing problem with [Optimization.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/Optimization/stable/); - compare an optimized policy with no intervention and a fixed reference policy; and - state the objective, bounds, and limitations that determine what an “optimal” intervention means. ## Model assumptions and classification The model is deterministic, continuous in time, continuous in state, and population based. It retains the closed, homogeneous SIR assumptions of @kermack1927 and adds a temporary intervention that reduces transmission by a fraction $v(t)$. This is a scenario model, not an individual-level simulation: the callback changes one population-level coefficient at specified times. The baseline is $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, $N=1000$, $\beta=0.05$, $c=10$, and $\gamma=0.25$. The intervention used below reduces transmission by $v_{\max}=0.5$ for a fixed duration of 10 time units. The decision variable is only the start time $t_1$, bounded to $0\leq t_1\leq25$. More general time-varying controls belong in the advanced [InfiniteOpt/SDDP unit](../appendices/08-advanced-optimal-control.html). ## Equations We add cumulative incidence $C(t)$ as a bookkeeping state. During a policy window, transmission is multiplied by $1-v(t)$: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dt} &= -\beta c(1-v(t))\frac{SI}{N},\\ \frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt} &= \beta c(1-v(t))\frac{SI}{N}-\gamma I,\\ \frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dt} &= \gamma I,\\ \frac{\mathrm dC}{\mathrm dt} &= \beta c(1-v(t))\frac{SI}{N}. \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-intervention-sir} For a rectangular policy, $$ v(t;t_1)= \begin{cases} v_{\max},&t_1\leq t ``` A callback-defined intervention scenario compared with no intervention. ::: ::: ### A bounded Optimization.jl problem Now the scenario function becomes the objective. `OptimizationFunction` with `AutoFiniteDiff()` differentiates the scalar objective by finite differences, while `Fminbox(LBFGS())` enforces the explicit lower and upper bounds. The optimizer only chooses $t_1$; it does not decide whether the intervention is ethical, feasible to deliver, or appropriate for the model. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function final_incidence(x, _) solution = run_scenario(x[1]) return Array(solution)[4, end] end objective = OptimizationFunction(final_incidence, AutoFiniteDiff()) optimization_problem = OptimizationProblem( objective, [reference_start], nothing; lb = [0.0], ub = [25.0], ) optimization_solution = solve( optimization_problem, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 30, ) optimal_start = optimization_solution.u[1] optimal_solution = run_scenario(optimal_start) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` retcode: Success Interpolation: 1st order linear t: 95-element Vector{Float64}: 0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 3.5 4.0 4.5 ⋮ 41.0 41.5 42.0 42.5 43.0 43.5 44.0 44.5 45.0 u: 95-element Vector{Vector{Float64}}: [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0] [987.3708077772923, 11.299550983027808, 1.3296412396798327, 2.6291922227076383] [984.4093729570689, 12.759075460611204, 2.8315515823198423, 5.590627042931044] [981.0774035610079, 14.395804457229898, 4.52679198176206, 8.922596438991958] [977.3332016620534, 16.228146580360058, 6.43865175758647, 12.666798337946528] [973.1316388125458, 18.27557198561527, 8.592789201838702, 16.868361187453967] [968.4242212073968, 20.558425388134197, 11.01735340446879, 21.575778792602982] [963.1592706992523, 23.09765186712193, 13.743077433625668, 26.840729300747597] [957.2822512701779, 25.91441784844529, 16.80333088137662, 32.717748729821906] [950.7362723645176, 29.02961005503149, 20.234117580450746, 39.26372763548223] ⋮ [369.51050655686157, 28.44465080693714, 602.0448426362009, 620.4894934431379] [366.934553877266, 27.522768664973952, 605.5426774577596, 623.0654461227335] [364.4599615300239, 26.613958824924836, 608.9260796450509, 625.5400384699756] [362.0836722365037, 25.719559818176158, 612.1967679453197, 627.9163277634958] [359.8026263605876, 24.840754278575783, 615.3566193608362, 630.1973736394119] [357.61377402724895, 23.978576316461474, 618.4076496562892, 632.3862259727506] [355.51408624590715, 23.13391999391043, 621.351993760182, 634.4859137540923] [353.50056258255466, 22.307545916421088, 624.1918915010239, 636.4994374174448] [351.5702406004708, 21.500090657784998, 626.9296687417437, 638.4297593995286] ``` ::: ::: The bounded problem can be inspected on a grid as well as by the optimizer. The grid is a diagnostic, not a replacement for the optimization API. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} candidate_starts = collect(0.0:1.0:25.0) candidate_objectives = [final_incidence([start], nothing) for start in candidate_starts] objective_at_optimum = final_incidence([optimal_start], nothing) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 638.4297593995286 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ch11-optimization .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (900, 450)) ax = Axis( fig[1, 1], xlabel = "intervention start time", ylabel = "final cumulative incidence", title = "Bounded timing optimization", ) lines!(ax, candidate_starts, candidate_objectives, color = :darkorange) scatter!(ax, [optimal_start], [objective_at_optimum], color = :firebrick, markersize = 14, label = "optimizer") axislegend(ax) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch11-optimization .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Final cumulative incidence as intervention start time varies. ::: ::: ## Validation The state equations imply $S+I+R=N$ and $C$ is nondecreasing. The scenario callback should also reduce final incidence relative to no intervention for this parameter choice. Finally, the optimizer result must lie inside the declared box and agree with a nearby grid value. ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} optimal_array = Array(optimal_solution(time_grid)) conservation_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(optimal_array[1:3, :]; dims = 1)) .- baseline.N)) incidence_is_monotone = all(diff(optimal_array[4, :]) .>= -1e-10) grid_minimum = minimum(candidate_objectives) @assert conservation_error < 1e-6 @assert incidence_is_monotone @assert 0.0 <= optimal_start <= 25.0 @assert objective_at_optimum <= grid_minimum + 1.0 @assert optimal_array[4, end] < baseline_array[4, end] (conservation_error = conservation_error, optimal_start = optimal_start, final_incidence_without_policy = baseline_array[4, end], final_incidence_with_policy = optimal_array[4, end]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (conservation_error = 4.547473508864641e-13, optimal_start = 13.840352420007697, final_incidence_without_policy = 785.4841454123757, final_incidence_with_policy = 638.4297593995286) ``` ::: ::: ## Interpretation and limitations The result is an optimal start time **conditional on** a fixed 50% reduction, a fixed ten-unit duration, a homogeneous closed population, perfect timing, and the final-incidence objective. It is not a universal recommendation. Changing the cost of intervention, adding a peak-infection penalty, or penalizing delayed action changes the problem. The rectangular callback also creates an idealized instantaneous policy switch; a ramp-up, adherence model, or stochastic transmission would be a different model. This chapter uses a small bounded problem intentionally; continuous controls, path constraints, and multistage uncertainty are deferred to the advanced optimal-control appendix. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch11-ex1} Modify `run_scenario` to compare reductions of `0.25`, `0.50`, and `0.75`. For each reduction, optimize the start time using the same bounds. Report the start time and final incidence, and explain why the best timing need not be the time at which infectious prevalence is largest. ### Exercise 2 {#ch11-ex2} Define a new scalar objective $C(T)+\lambda\int v(t)\,\mathrm dt$ for a nonnegative cost weight $\lambda$. With a variable intervention duration, describe which additional bound or constraint prevents the optimizer from selecting an unrealistically long intervention. Implement the objective for two values of $\lambda$ and compare the resulting policy choices. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/11-interventions-and-optimization.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/11-interventions-and-optimization.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/11-interventions-and-optimization.jl)
